mcqs.question: What does the expression `1 << 3` produce, and why is it useful for bit idioms?
options: The number 3 itself, unchanged
The number of set bits in 3
An integer with a single 1 at position 3 and 0s elsewhere, usable as a mask
The bitwise NOT of 3
mcqs.explanation: Shifting the literal 1 left by 3 places a single 1 at bit position 3, giving a mask that touches only that one position when combined with AND, OR, or XOR — the building block every get/set/clear/toggle idiom uses. It has nothing to do with the value 3, its popcount, or its complement.

mcqs.question: Why does clear_bit use `x & ~(1 << i)` instead of `x & (1 << i)`?
options: Both expressions clear bit i identically
`x & (1 << i)` would clear every bit except bit i, and set bit i to whatever it already was
`x & ~(1 << i)` inverts the entire mask so every bit except i stays as it was, and ANDing forces only bit i to 0
The NOT is only needed when i is 0
mcqs.explanation: Inverting the single-bit mask turns it into all-1s except a 0 at position i; ANDing with that preserves every other bit (AND with 1 is a no-op) while forcing position i to 0. Without the NOT, ANDing against a mask that's mostly 0s would zero out nearly everything, which is the opposite of what clearing one bit needs.

mcqs.question: In the range mask idiom `((1 << (hi - lo + 1)) - 1) << lo`, what is the role of subtracting 1 after the shift?
options: It shifts the mask down by one position
It converts a single high bit into a contiguous block of that many 1s below it
It clears bit lo specifically
It has no effect and is only there for readability
mcqs.explanation: `1 << k` is a single 1 at position k with all 0s below it; subtracting 1 borrows through every one of those lower zero bits, flipping them all to 1 and leaving a block of k ones — the standard "k ones in a row" idiom. It doesn't shift anything or target bit lo specifically, and it is very much load-bearing, not cosmetic.

mcqs.question: You want to set bit i to a boolean value v that might be 0 or 1. Why is `x |= (1 << i)` wrong when v is 0?
options: OR can only ever set a bit to 1, so it silently fails to clear the bit when v is 0
The expression throws an error when v is 0
OR works correctly for both 0 and 1 as long as i is valid
The bug only appears when i equals 0
mcqs.explanation: OR-ing with a 1 can only ever turn a bit on or leave it on — it has no mechanism to turn a bit off, so if the intent was to write v=0 into that position, the OR silently does nothing when the bit was already 1. The fix is to clear the bit first, then OR in the shifted value of v; the bug is real for any i, not just i=0, and nothing throws.

mcqs.question: For an inclusive bit range [lo, hi], how many bits does the range actually span?
options: hi - lo
hi - lo + 1
hi + lo
Always exactly one bit, since lo and hi mark the same position
mcqs.explanation: An inclusive range from lo to hi covers both endpoints, so it spans hi - lo + 1 positions — for lo=2, hi=4 that's bits 2, 3, and 4, three bits, matching 4-2+1. Using hi - lo without the +1 undercounts by exactly one bit, a classic off-by-one that silently drops the highest bit of the range.
